speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have filed these Parliamentary Questions (PQs) relating to the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will respond to these five questions together so that I can give and provide a more holistic reply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the bases and the considerations in the design of the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Prime Minister and I have shared the Government’s considerations in designing the Jobseeker Support scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we wanted to create a better alternative to unemployment insurance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have seen from other countries how unemployment insurance can make it more attractive for individuals to stay unemployed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also heard feedback from employers about rising business costs and we do not want employers to offset the costs of an insurance scheme by cutting wages or by stopping the practice of retrenchment benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is why we searched for a better alternative to minimise the negative outcomes that we have seen elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our objective is to support involuntarily unemployed individuals to rebound into jobs that better match and fit their skills and experience, instead of rushing into ill-fitting jobs due to financial pressures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at the same time, from the Forward Singapore exercise, we have heard Singaporeans share that personal responsibility should remain a cornerstone in our social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, the scheme should minimise the potential moral hazard by supporting jobseekers to regain employment and not continued unemployment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Jobseekers will need to play their part, to take responsibility for their actions and make an effort to bounce back into work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the Government’s part, we will continue to strongly support jobseekers through employment facilitation and training programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will next answer questions on who will qualify for the Jobseeker Support scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is slightly above the median monthly income of resident workers and it is the group that is more likely to face some financial pressures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the condition “residing in a property with an annual value of $25,000” was determined.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Annual value is used as a proxy to determine households’ wealth for various Government support schemes that provide higher benefits to individuals or households with lower means.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The threshold of $25,000 for the Jobseeker Support scheme is aligned with other schemes, such as the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Voucher scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This covers about 75% of residential properties, including all Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how applicants’ eligibility will be assessed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: All Jobseeker Support applications will be assessed via a system that comprises automated checks using available Government data and further verification checks done by a dedicated Workforce Singapore (WSG) team.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For individuals who do not meet the eligibility criteria, appeals will be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Hazel Poa also asked why Permanent Residents (PRs) are eligible for the scheme alongside Singapore Citizens (SCs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is no different from other employment facilitation programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, SCs and PRs receive the same support under WSG programmes, such as career matching services and Career Conversion Programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to stress that Singaporeans will always be at the heart of Government policies, even while we welcome those who can commit and contribute to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our citizens receive the most support and benefit in several areas, including housing, healthcare, education and parenthood.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But PRs have expressed their commitment to Singapore and contribute to our strengths as a society and economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, likewise, we should also support our PRs who fall onto hard times to get into good jobs so that they can support themselves and contribute to our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will now move on to questions about the payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked why the payments are stepped down with time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have designed the payout schedule to provide a higher payout in the earlier months to provide greater upfront assurance to jobseekers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These payouts are gradually reduced from the second month onwards to incentivise jobseekers to start work earlier if they find and land on a good-fitting job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not want them to delay their return into the workforce as it will diminish their employability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, as the scheme is designed to encourage individuals to find a job with good fit and be retained in the job, those who have received payouts will not be able to make another application within three years of their last payout.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I must emphasise that the total payout of up to $6,000 should not be viewed in isolation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It actually complements the Government’s broader ecosystem of support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Henry Kwek had asked about whether beneficiaries of the scheme can also benefit from other financial assistance schemes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While the Jobseeker Support scheme is not designed as a form of social assistance for households with greater financial needs, beneficiaries are still entitled to receive support from the Government’s social assistance schemes where eligible, such as ComCare Short-to-Medium Term Assistance and the GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we encourage jobseekers to actively explore ways to upskill, to reskill themselves to bounce back into better jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Prime Minister had said that a major reset is needed as we chart Singapore's way forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remember even during my first term as an MP in this House, this was also raised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I am glad that the Government has finally made the move.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question is: under this scheme, the criteria have been tightly structured, such as with the salary cap of $5,000, the annual value of not more than $25,000, the financial relief is also for a maximum of six months.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Minister how the Ministry determines the sufficiency of this scheme to help jobseekers and whether it will achieve the outcomes that we have set out to achieve?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We started looking at it a number of years ago and, as a result of our Forward Singapore conversations, we have also sought feedback from many of our fellow Singaporeans on the design of the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also learnt from many other countries, in terms of their own unemployment benefits for their respective citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we eventually sized up the Jobseeker Support scheme, which is really about also renewing and refreshing the social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we look ahead, the pace of change and disruptions will only accelerate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We may see a higher incidence of job displacements due to factors beyond an individual's control and even as they build their career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, because of the multiple dialogues we have had, we have heard calls from Singaporeans for greater assurance in dealing with involuntary job loss.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the reset, as I have mentioned, is now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The scheme marks a paradigm shift for the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have taken the time to study the scheme carefully to ensure that we avoid the pitfalls seen in unemployment insurance schemes overseas where it can lull individuals into a false sense of security by making it more attractive for them to stay unemployed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We took in the different feedback from our tripartite partners, businesses and the public in the eventual design of the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And having said that, our assurance is that we will continue to review the parameters of the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we have sized it for the lower- to middle-income worker earning up to $5,000 per month before becoming involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, this is sized at just above the median monthly income of resident workers, as this is the group that is more likely to face some financial pressure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as I have said, for the six-month duration of payouts, we think it provides sufficient assurance for jobseekers to find good fitting jobs and at the same time, it encourages them to re-enter the workforce in a timely manner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to reiterate that we will regularly review the scheme to ensure that we provide the necessary and needed support for the involuntarily unemployed residents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I appreciate the design of the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme as our people need not pay an insurance premium to benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also note that many Singaporeans have family members who are PRs and they will benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The first part on eligibility checks, as I have shared earlier on, based on whatever Government data we have, will be automatic.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But for those who want to appeal, we will consider them on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has said that in this case, they have decided to extend the same benefits to PRs and SCs and quoted a few examples where it is also same benefits for both groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But at the same time, we do have schemes that differentiate between these two groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, how does the Government decide which scheme will give the same benefits for SCs and PRs and which will be differentiated?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In certain industries, where the pace of change and disruption is more frequent, the workers in those industries may experience retrenchment more frequently than those in other industries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, would the Minister also consider this on a case-by-case basis?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For her first point on PRs receiving similar treatment and quantum of benefits as SCs, I hope that the Member appreciates the fact that this is a Jobseeker Support scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is to incentivise the jobseeker to actively go for interviews, update their resumes and go for courses to upgrade themselves to get employed back into the workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, in such circumstance, PRs can receive the same treatment and quantum of benefits because such schemes, if we support them, it will enable them to stay employable and continue to contribute to Singapore economically.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And it also encourages the individuals to take responsibility for their own retirement adequacy and their own income security and, with them gainfully employed, ultimately, we hope that they will also not burden the rest of us as a society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the three-year window, this is to nudge and encourage our jobseekers to use this Jobseeker Support scheme to find better fitting jobs, and not rush into an ill-fitting job so as to get retrenched, displaced or unemployed within a short period of time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But having said that, exactly to Ms Poa's point, the pace of disruptions and change, indeed, they are both accelerating.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those who are involuntarily unemployed as a result of circumstances beyond their control, we are prepared to look at it on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In instances where recipients of the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme may face immediate financial difficulties, why did the Ministry decide not to streamline short-term financial support with the scheme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, will the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) work with the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and the SSOs to process the Jobseeker Support scheme together with other financial assistance schemes?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have alluded to, the Jobseeker Support scheme is not a social assistance scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is meant to nudge our residents towards a positive behaviour of ensuring that they continue not to be disenfranchised, but to actively seek out a job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And this sits on top of other social assistance schemes that are administered by MSF and a host of other agencies that the Government has.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, for residents who are mature workers aged 40 and above, who are already on the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, this sits on top of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps I can use this as an illustration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If he is drawing a salary of $5,000 and he is on this SkillsFuture Level-Up course, he draws an allowance of $2,500 a month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I wanted to give that archetype to illustrate to Mr Yip the potential amounts that an actively engaged mature jobseeker who is also upgrading himself will be able to access via these grants from the Government.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So, therefore, my point is, now that we have set the $5,000 and the annual value of $25,000, how can MOM ensure that these PMEs, if they are really financially strapped, are not left out and will be able to bounce back and go into the next job.

The second supplementary question is with regard to the JobSeeker Support Scheme, whether MOM will have some form of monitoring and enforcement to make sure that employers who already currently provide retrenchment benefits in severance packages in their employment contracts or even in their collective agreements, do not exploit this scheme and, therefore, cut back or reduce those other payments?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We acknowledge many Members in the House for putting up the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I was looking back at all the notes, I think it went back to as early as 2014, about a decade ago.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, thank you to many of our labour MPs and Members of this House, some of whom are not here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There was a Mr Azmoon Ahmad, from before, who also proposed the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I want to thank them for proposing this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, when we sized up the scheme, we wanted to try to reach out to the lower- and middle-income group.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our starting point is to try to support the lower- and middle-income workers, who may face more financial pressures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While we acknowledge that some PMETs at the higher level could also face pressures as well, given their runway, given the buffer that they have, for a start, I think that they have a slightly better buffer compared to this group of lower- and middle-income workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like I said, we will continue to review it and to see how we can be even more sensitive to the needs of more workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to the Member's second point about how we ensure that employers do not then roll back or dial back on the retrenchment benefit, we have to work very closely with the Labour Movement and with our tripartite partners to make sure that this is not against the spirit of wanting to help our workers to bounce back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The good momentum that we have achieved thus far, in ensuring that there is a fair treatment for all workers, will continue to be honoured and followed through.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, will any tax increases be needed for this?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Did the Government consider making this an unemployment insurance scheme so that it is more fiscally sustainable over the long term?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That is what the Workers' Party (WP) proposed in our version of the redundancy insurance scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to reiterate that this is not an unemployment insurance scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is very different from what the WP has suggested.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also taken feedback from our workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The feedback that we have obtained is that there are cost pressures that are experienced by businesses and workers wanting to be able to have more take-home earnings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, when we looked at the entire landscape and we also studied other countries' experiences, for a start, we felt that this is the most nuanced way forward – with the Government taking the burden of providing these jobseekers, who actively want to look for jobs, with the assistance to tide them over this particular period.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The way the scheme has been sized up, 60% of the involuntarily unemployed workers will benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, about close to 60% of workers get back into a job within six months of being involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Depending on how the scheme continues to evolve, we will continue to review the parameters to make sure that it supports and it is sensitive to the needs of residents who are involuntarily unemployed.
